triage.name: Retinopathy of prematurity
triage.reason: Premature infant found on screening fundoscopic exam; diagnosis is made by eye exam rather than interview, so it is a weaker but still usable case.

demographics: Occurs almost exclusively in premature infants
Highest incidence in extremely premature and very low birth weight infants
Screening recommended for infants born ≤30 weeks gestational age or <1500 g

chief_complaints.text: The eye doctor said the blood vessels in my baby's eyes look abnormal.
My baby doesn't seem to look at my face or follow objects.
One of my baby's pupils looks white in photos.

hpi.onset: Not noticed by parents; detected on routine retinopathy of prematurity screening eye exam
hpi.duration: Usually detected between 31 and 36 weeks postmenstrual age, or 4–6 weeks after birth
hpi.progression: Most mild cases regress spontaneously; some progress to more advanced stages with extraretinal proliferation, traction, and retinal detachment
hpi.quality: Not applicable; baby has no pain complaint
hpi.timing: Detected on scheduled screening, not by symptoms

associated_symptoms.text: My baby doesn't seem to look at my face or follow objects.
My baby's eyes sometimes look crossed.
One of my baby's pupils looks white in photos.
My baby's eyes make jerky movements.

pertinent_negatives: Appropriate birth weight for gestational age
Family history of hereditary retinal disease

positives.text: The eye doctor said the blood vessels in my baby's eyes look abnormal.

atypical.how_it_differs: Older children with regressed or treated ROP present with decreased vision, strabismus, nystagmus, or retinal detachment rather than active vascular proliferation.

general.mild: Well-appearing premature infant; no systemic signs of eye disease; alert and active.
general.moderate: Well-appearing premature infant; may not fix and follow objects but otherwise no systemic signs.
general.severe: Well-appearing premature infant; may have strabismus or nystagmus; no systemic signs.
general.critical: Well-appearing premature infant; may have leukocoria and visual inattention; no systemic signs.

findings.finding: Abnormal retinal vascular morphology at the junction of vascular and avascular retina.
Extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation extending from the ridge into the vitreous.

findings.maneuver: Perform indirect ophthalmoscopy of the posterior pole
findings.finding: Dilated retinal veins in at least two quadrants.

findings.maneuver: Perform indirect ophthalmoscopy of the posterior pole
findings.finding: Tortuous retinal arteries in at least two quadrants.

findings.maneuver: Perform indirect ophthalmoscopy with scleral depression

findings.finding: Total retinal detachment with retrolental membrane (stage 5).

findings.maneuver: Assess red reflex with direct ophthalmoscope
findings.finding: Absent red reflex; pupil appears white.

findings.maneuver: Perform corneal light reflex test (Hirschberg) and cover test
Perform slit lamp examination (or penlight) for anterior chamber
findings.finding: No cells or flare in anterior chamber.

findings.text: Demarcation line between vascular and avascular retina (stage 1)
Extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation extending from the ridge (stage 3)
Dilated and tortuous posterior retinal vessels in at least two quadrants (plus disease)
Total retinal detachment with retrolental membrane (stage 5)

imaging.preferred_when: Media opacity (e.g., vitreous hemorrhage, cataract) prevents fundoscopic view
Equivocal findings or suspected plus disease

initial.why: Screening for retinopathy of prematurity in at-risk infants; allows remote reading or documentation.

confirmatory.why: Definitive diagnosis and staging by direct visualization of the retina; required for treatment decisions.

supporting.why: Clarifies equivocal findings or suspected plus disease.
supporting.only_if: equivocal findings or suspected plus disease

supporting.why: Evaluates retinal detachment when media opacity limits fundoscopy.
supporting.only_if: media opacity (vitreous hemorrhage, cataract) prevents fundoscopic view

not_indicated.why: No role in diagnosis or management of retinopathy of prematurity.
No role unless systemic illness is suspected.
No role in diagnosing retinopathy of prematurity.
Only if sepsis is suspected, not for retinopathy of prematurity itself.

decision_points: Initial screening exam at 31 weeks postmenstrual age or 4 weeks chronological age, whichever is later, for infants born ≤30 weeks GA or <1500 g.
Follow-up intervals based on initial findings: 1 week or more frequently for immature vessels in zone I; 1-2 weeks for stage 1 or 2 without plus disease in zone II; 2-3 weeks if regressing.

Treatment (laser photocoagulation or anti-VEGF injection) is indicated for type 1 ROP: zone I any stage with plus disease, zone I stage 3 without plus disease, or zone II stage 2 or 3 with plus disease.
Refer to pediatric ophthalmologist for all at-risk infants.

criteria.name: International Classification of Retinopathy of Prematurity (ICROP)
criteria.summary: Categorizes ROP by location (zones I-III), severity (stages 1-5), extent (clock hours), and presence of plus disease (dilated, tortuous posterior vessels).

differential.name: Retinoblastoma
differential.why_considered: Leukocoria or abnormal red reflex in an infant
differential.trigger: Leukocoria or a white pupil in any infant, especially if not extremely premature

history: Family history of retinoblastoma in about 10%
No history of extreme prematurity or prolonged oxygen therapy
exam: Retinal mass with calcification on dilated exam
labs: Genetic testing for RB1 mutation if family history
imaging: Ocular ultrasound shows calcified intraocular mass
MRI of brain and orbits if optic nerve extension suspected

differential.name: Persistent fetal vasculature
differential.why_considered: Leukocoria and retrolental membrane in an infant

imaging: Ocular ultrasound shows persistent hyaloid artery remnant
No peripheral avascular retina as in ROP

differential.name: Familial exudative vitreoretinopathy
differential.why_considered: Peripheral retinal avascularity and neovascularization in an infant

history: Family history of retinal detachment or childhood blindness
labs: Genetic testing for FZD4, LRP5, TSPAN12, NDP mutations
imaging: Fluorescein angiography shows leakage and nonperfusion, often in a similar pattern to ROP but without prematurity

differential.name: Coats disease
differential.why_considered: Leukocoria and retinal detachment in a child

imaging: Fluorescein angiography shows telangiectatic vessels with leakage

history: May have family history or intrauterine infection
imaging: Ocular ultrasound shows normal posterior segment if view obscured

severity.mild: Stage 1 or 2 retinopathy of prematurity in zone II or III without plus disease; usually regresses spontaneously without treatment
severity.moderate: Stage 3 retinopathy of prematurity in zone II without plus disease, or pre-plus disease; requires more frequent monitoring and may progress to treatment-requiring disease
severity.severe: Type 1 retinopathy of prematurity (zone I any stage with plus disease, zone I stage 3 without plus, or zone II stage 2 or 3 with plus disease) requiring treatment; or partial retinal detachment (stage 4)

red_flags.finding: Plus disease (dilated, tortuous posterior vessels in at least two quadrants)
red_flags.meaning: Indicates active disease requiring urgent ophthalmology evaluation and likely treatment
Higher risk of progression and poor outcome; treatment threshold lower
May require more frequent monitoring or early treatment
Advanced disease; needs immediate pediatric ophthalmology referral
Possible advanced ROP or another serious eye condition; requires urgent exam

complications.name: Retinal detachment
clues: Total retinal detachment with retrolental membrane

complications.name: Amblyopia
clues: Often associated with strabismus or refractive error

special_populations.differences: All cases occur in premature infants; risk and severity increase with lower gestational age and birth weight. Screening is based on these factors.
Older children with regressed or treated ROP present with decreased vision, strabismus, nystagmus, or retinal detachment rather than active vascular proliferation.

key_questions.question: What did the eye doctor tell you about your baby's eyes?
key_questions.looking_for: Report of abnormal retinal blood vessels, stage, zone, and plus disease on screening exam

key_questions.question: At what gestational age was your baby born?
key_questions.looking_for: Gestational age ≤30 weeks; extreme prematurity greatly increases risk

key_questions.question: What was your baby's birth weight?
Did your baby need oxygen or a breathing machine after birth? For how long?
key_questions.looking_for: Prolonged or fluctuating supplemental oxygen exposure

key_questions.question: Has your baby received any blood transfusions?
key_questions.looking_for: Blood transfusion as a risk factor

key_questions.question: Has your baby had any previous eye exams? When were they and what did they show?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior ROP stage, progression, regression, or treatment

key_questions.question: Does your baby seem to look at your face or follow objects?
key_questions.looking_for: Visual inattention or poor fixation suggesting advanced disease

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any white pupil, unusual eye movements, or crossed eyes?
Is there a family history of childhood eye problems, blindness, or retinal detachment?
Were there any problems during the pregnancy or delivery?
key_questions.looking_for: Congenital infection or other causes of retinopathy

reasoning_points: Born at ≤30 weeks gestation or birth weight <1500 g, meeting screening criteria
Prolonged or fluctuating supplemental oxygen exposure
Dilated fundus exam shows peripheral avascular retina with a demarcation line/ridge and possible extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation
Plus disease: dilated and tortuous posterior retinal vessels in at least two quadrants indicates active disease
No signs of retinoblastoma (e.g., no calcified mass, no family history, extreme prematurity)
Staging according to ICROP (zones, stages, plus disease) guides management
Type 1 ROP meets treatment threshold (zone I any stage with plus, zone I stage 3 without plus, zone II stage 2/3 with plus)
Other risk factors include sepsis, blood transfusion, poor postnatal weight gain

easy: Extremely premature infant born at 24 weeks with birth weight 650 g
Clear history of prolonged supplemental oxygen
Screening exam shows zone II stage 3 with plus disease
No competing diagnosis; classic textbook ROP
medium: Moderately premature infant born at 30 weeks and 1400 g
Stage 2 ROP without plus disease, requiring serial exams
Pre-plus disease or borderline zone II/III disease
Some risk factors present but less severe
hard: Borderline screening criteria: born at 31-32 weeks or birth weight just above 1500 g
Leukocoria or retinal detachment raising concern for retinoblastoma or other causes
Unclear oxygen history or missing prior exam records
Advanced stage 4/5 ROP with total retinal detachment requiring differentiation from persistent fetal vasculature
